Every house has a drawer that refuses to be anything. Not silverware, not napkins—just the place where objects go when they're too stubborn to throw away and too useless to keep anywhere honest. My grandmother called hers the "maybe drawer." Everything in it was a maybe. A key that might open something. A battery that might still have a charge. A flashlight that works only if you shake it, which is also a metaphor, if you want one. A screw, and somewhere in the house, a thing that had lost its screw, still functioning, holding on, one fastener short of ruin.

I opened it the other day looking for scissors and found instead a small archaeology. A birthday candle, pinched at the wick from a wish made years ago. A rubber band, brittle now, that snapped when I touched it. A photograph of a dog I don't remember, though the back says "Rusty, 1987" in my father's handwriting, so he must have been ours, or almost ours, or a neighbor's we borrowed on Sundays.

The drawer is a museum of postponed decisions. Someone, someday, will have to open it and say no to everything at once. I hope they don't. I hope they find the scissors they were looking for, and the photograph of Rusty, and sit down on the old kitchen floor to wonder who this small dog was, and why we kept him in a drawer all these years, patient as a saint, waiting to be remembered.
